tldr: Headlines across nine countries uniformly lead with an injury count, with several UK and Australian titles foregrounding a critically injured five-year-old child; the driver's arrest appears in roughly half the headlines. The police non-terror caveat — universal in body text — is absent from every headline.

evidence.quote: Five-year-old girl in critical condition after car hits
Five-year-old girl is in an induced coma after she and nine
Ten injured in Australia as car crashes into crowd
Ten people injured, P-plater charged after car crashes
Driver arrested after car crashes into rugby league fans

single_outlet_findings.finding: Pipeline misassignment: headline ('Three in hospital after car crashes into building in central London', dated 2024-11-12) is a separate London incident unrelated to Newcastle.
Only headline to use 'induced coma' — the most medically specific and emotionally charged phrase in the corpus, foregrounding severity beyond the bare injury count.
Only headline to use 'Children among' (plural), broadening the vulnerability frame beyond the single five-year-old foregrounded by other outlets.
Only headline to reproduce an emotive characterisation ('horrible incident') as a quoted label rather than a factual description.

bottom_line: Headline-layer coverage reduces the incident to two flat registers — injury count and driver arrest — while the police non-terror caveat that dominates every body text is invisible to any reader who does not click through.
